p: Okay, great. Uhm, and then just moving really quickly to the Chief Savings Officer. What type of target was the CSO given by OMB? Was it the same percentage?
That is correct, yes.
So, the $1.5 and then the $2.5 for FY27 right?
That’s correct.
Okay and where has the agency found the savings? I know the report is coming this week and how will it impact the city’s - the agencies programs and performances?

So, we are continuing to review our agency's budget to identify savings. Our goal is to try to minimize or have no impact on services as the Mayor has directed. And so, we’re looking under every cushion and seat to see where we can find any savings that we can find and we’re hopeful that we will. Uhm, and meet the target by this week.

Okay, perfect and definitely want to emphasize we definitely want to make sure that the services are not cut. So, if there’s challenges there obviously to let us know that as well. And when is the agency - it’s submitting the proposal to OMB Friday, correct?
That’s correct.
Okay, perfect. Thank you. Thank you Chair.

Thank you. Uhm, I’m going to let Council Member Joseph go because I’m about to talk about Summer Rising and she has a whole host of questions for Summer Rising because uhm, I just can’t

anymore but I guess my question just to kind of frame it is to just thinking about uhm, how are we going to move forward, use the feedback from young people and families to kind of start reshaping what Summer Rising could be? I know we have a new Commissioner and she is doing her own evaluations but would love to just hear your thoughts on like how are you going to be moving forward to like reshape it? Because I know like some of my bigger issues and since you’re new, I don’t think you heard all of them before. So I’ll just go for a few of just thinking about how are we you know, really taking the feedback from young people, especially middle school students who said that they did not want to sit in a classroom all day and they wanted it to be there Fridays, which was why when we cut Fridays that was crazy for me thinking about uhm, when you only have the flexibility to go on trips on Friday? That really makes it crazy for the city because we have issues with buses. So, all of the kids that’s in camp, 90,000 children, 100,000 kids can’t be on the subway on a Friday. And so, like how do we really start to look at this program and reshape it so that it can be not only just fun but inclusive of learning and

showing all of the different components of not just sitting in a classroom from 8-12 to say that that’s the only way young people could learn. And so, I would love to just hear your thoughts about how like what and how will we use this summer to kind of evaluate and move into a place that really honors the work of the youth educators who is doing this work and bringing their expertise and not just kind of having this theory that only teachers can teach young people.
I’m going to start off -
You got to push the button.

Yeah sorry. I’m going to start off and then I’m going to pass it over to folks who are running the program and have a more specific answer but I can tell you that there has been a range of feedback that we have gotten from people loving Summer Rising and for people who have not liked Summer Rising. But at the core, I think there is a continued commitment for us to make sure that young people are learning and developing throughout the school year. And then that could be done and achieved through a range of mediums, right? And I think - I love what you were saying earlier

Chair Stevens that it met the moment for COVID and we have to adapt. And so, some of the preliminary feed that we’ve gotten is exactly that. That what does learning look like outside of the classroom? And so, you’re going to hear from Daniel who is going to speak a little bit about how we’ve included career exploration. How we’ve increased trips.
I heard about those already.

In order to be able to do that but my charge right now is to stand up some models right in the next few months that we can implement and test out because the truth is also that the data is showing that young people who have 20 days or more in Summer Rising are gaining academically and in social emotional. So, we want to hold onto that. So, we don’t want to throw out the baby with the bath water but we do want to make adaptations based on what we’re hearing about how learning should happen for young people, specifically in the summer. So, my hope is to set up again some pilots and to test some things out so that next year, we can have a kind of a variety of options for us to choose from.
Absolutely.
That are resourced and sustainable. I said that for Nevita.

Good afternoon Chair. We have been part of this conversation for a number of years and I think what’s valuable here is that we’ve listened to your feedback and year to year we’ve strived to make continuous quality improvements through this process. Year one of Summer Rising is not year five of Summer Rising. It is adamantly clear, the demand is still there. Families still want services and we want holistic services and I’m including we, as the parent as well. And we look forward to ongoing conversations on how we can make this model better. Because the reality is, a centralized support system that thinks about the whole child is vital to the summer and we want to ensure that with all the learnings and all the things that we’ve gained experience on from the CBO’s onto the families and to the work that we do in collaboration with Public Schools continues that.

Absolutely, I mean again, I’ve said this so many times. I think that there’s a lot of things that we can pull from Summer Rising

that like went well. Like one of the things like being able to serve students with disabilities. That’s something that we’ve been able to really do and now that we can do that, like how do we multiply that? We want to see that. We want to see - you know I remember working before Summer Rising where every school had to be closed. Clearly that wasn’t the case, where now we know that the schools can be open. So, I think that there’s a lot of things here that we’ve learned and we’ve obviously changed but I think that we still have a lot of growing to do but I’m going to shut up and pass it over to Council Member Joseph because I gave her a whole bunch of questions and so, there you go. And she has her own feedback because we’ve been tag teaming this for the last four years.

Yeah, we have been tag teaming and we have seen lots of improvements right from when I started as an educator in the classroom, the first year they kicked off Summer Rising, I had just won my primary. I was leaving teaching and going to become a Council Member and I opened the first one with then Mayor de Blasio and then Chancellor Porter but we’ve seen a lot of changes and

we’ve asked for a lot and you guys have stepped up. So, we want to publicly say thank you especially for me with the foster youth.
Yeah, thank you.

Especially for me with the foster youth. With the foster youth being included, that was so personal for me and our students in temporary housing, that was also very personal to me as being an educator on the other side. However, there has been issues when we talked about attendance. So, my questions will be at along the line of assessment. How do we move forward? How do we tweak and make it better? Adding the social emotional learning was something we were pushing for a very long time to make it not just the standalone social, emotional learning but part of the curriculum. Right that it’s embedded in the curriculum. That it’s not a standalone. It’s throughout the whole day, to provide that support. So, I’m always wearing that educator hat. Forever an educator hat on to make sure those things are also implemented.

So, in 2027 we know we restored it and that was one thing. Once we saw those cuts, Council - Chair Stevens and I, we were in the streets yelling because we knew that the population that was targeted is some of our most vulnerable students who will - we don’t want them where they don’t want to be. That was it. So, that restoration was good. So, what metric was used - I’m going to go back. The PMMR indicated a fourth month actual of $113,376 youth K-8 attending the program, compared to $115,048 for the same time prior year. That’s about 1,672 youth or 1.5 percent less than the prior year. What’s happening in that area? Where are these kids? What are we doing to find them or are there other programs? Do you track them when they’re not in the system? You know how you track your students when they leave. Are you tracking them?

Yeah, so thank you for the question. So, one thing that makes Summer uniquely different from afterschool, that is not a mandated program and I think a key feature and something that we need to discuss in the future about what utilization really means and most importantly, what that means for families because we put access first

and ensuring that we can get to the most amount of families that have the opportunity to take advantage of this great program. Uhm, what we have noticed is this, right? Uhm restorations like this are generally informed by participation levels, program utilization and feedback from families in schools and providers about the importance of the extended programming. Summer Rising continues to be a critical support for working families and this restoration really reflects that continued demand for the resources. We really want to make sure that at an earlier point in time that this service was restored because it does impact ongoing recruitment efforts and stability for young people. So, ensuring early on that this money was available is a huge win for all of us in this sector.

And retention too. So, I talked about retention, how do you get the families through the door and we keep them there? What makes the family, such a huge number of families drop off in the program and how do we get them back, and how often do you look at the students that are on the

waitlist that you could rapidly fill in that spot when students leave the program?

So, what’s made this revamped version of Summer Rising is this centralized process where you have an active waitlist and you’re looking at this waitlist by the young people that are applying, where they’re coming from, if there are participants that have been a part of the year long services. So, there’s a real targeted approach. Another thing is that it’s really getting families to participate in those parent orientations. It’s making those connections. On the ground, right, what’s valuable is that there is that program director that meets that family. That they’re learning about the services, what’s offered and then that engagement throughout you know the application release, the selection and that communication all the way to the start of the program. If there’s some real concerns about their ability to attend, then you have that waitlist, right? That targeted approach and now, you can now build retention with a new family that’s just as interested and has been waiting all this time.

And with this model, what’s been amazing is that there’s families that have never gotten a chance to get in the door that now do this portal in My Schools.

I hear that a lot from - especially from my district that families who have applied, have never gotten in or if they’re on a waitlist they never hear from anyone, so we want to make sure this model is also doing outreach in real time as you’re looking at the attendance and looking at the whole program and say, hey, we have this amount of seats open here, there. How do we turn around rapidly for those on the waitlist? How many of the young people were elementary students and how many of them were middle school students that attended Summer Rising?
We can follow up with that.

Okay, thank you. That would be helpful then, you can also look at your data and make your assessments. Summer Rising continues to be a well-known program and numbers did exceed your targeted 100,000 month, a four month actual. What program changes have you made to attract middle school students? We

know that’s a population where they zero in on a lot to make sure they’re doing something for the summer and something fun.

Well, first and foremost, it’s ensuring that those hours are available, right? If a young person feels safe, that they can stay beyond 4:00 p.m. Monday through Thursday and that Fridays offer a full day of opportunities. A key component in that expansion of that career connective exploring futures component because young people at that age, they’re already thinking about the next wave right, workforce, becoming an SYEP participant. And this component that now we streamline across COMPASS from K-8 starts that conversation right and it actually contextualizes it. They have an opportunity to have in person experiences, go to visit the [INAUDIBLE 216:16] labs right? Go to visit all of these different businesses, industries even in their neighborhoods and having that - sparking that conversation, that curiosity at the age of you know 12 and up, i think is ideal because it’s the pathway that we want to ensure young people go towards and they have some agency on the planning, so it gives

them a little push and idea that it’s not just about being in the classroom but learning beyond.

And once you’re done with this programming, are you talking to young people to see feedback, surveys? I think you should also talk to them because my kid went to - he wouldn’t miss a day and I kept on telling Chair Stevens, we got to go see this program. He didn’t want to miss a day. He went every single day and the days - like, make my doctors appointments on another day mom. I don’t want to miss another day and there was an academic component to it and he was a middle school student. So, we should be capturing that data from young people to find out, what is it that’s capturing your attention? If it’s the financial literacy, the career connectedness, if it’s leaving the building, or that support that you probably provide through the social emotional learning. I think their voices are not used enough in making decisions for them but not with them. Uhm, what program was launched in 2020- what’s the average attendance for elementary and middle school attendees?

So, attendance in Summer Rising like I mentioned, is voluntary and it does vary by age group and elementary students typically attend more consistently, averaging several days per week across a seven week program. And middle school attendance is more valuable reflecting older students' schedules and preference. And we can provide the updated averages.

Yeah, that would be great and I know Chair Stevens touched upon this. Our students with disabilities, providing transportation to students with disabilities that want to stay longer, how is that going?

So, that is something that we’re working constantly with New York City Public Schools, it does require a lot of coordination centrally and at the site level. So, it is vital that folks understand like there are some advances that we’ve made but we continue to strive to improve.
Yes, our students with disabilities don’t just want to come for the academics. They also want to have fun too.
Agreed.

They definitely want to leave the building and be like their peers, right? So, I think that’s something that should be looked at with New York City Public Schools. How do we implement it? How do we make it sustainable for our young people that want to come to it in the summer time, to be in those buildings? I know they email me all day and I email you all day when they can’t get into those buildings. So, Chair Stevens, was that enough or should I add some more? No, I’m good. Thank you so much.

Okay, uhm so I’m going to jump into Beacon’s and Cornerstones and have some questions around that. Uhm, these are one of those programs that I think that I think are totally being underutilized and not getting enough attention and really great programs. The Beacon Community Centers are showing an increase in participation. The PMMR indicates that the the first four months of Fiscal 2026 beacon programs serve 37,851 youth and 7,394 adults, a 10 percent increase in the number of youth served and a 6 percent increase in the number of adults served when compared to some periods, the same period in

2025. This is partially due to the additional hours in programs for the Summer Safety Plan. The Beacon participants have increased but there has not been a change in contract rates that remain stagnant for more than 10 years. Is the agency considering a new RFP that would address the needs of the Beacons in Cornerstone Community Centers?

Chair Stevens, DYCD is continuing to currently look at the cost for it to be good in a Cornerstone model. We recognize that there are outdated procurements and we are currently looking at the program model, thinking about how we want to move going forward and what are the costs to do it. So, we are currently in that process.
And what does that process consist of?

It consists of stakeholder engagement, whether it be inclusive of you or others. Think about what is the model going to be? What are we doing? What have we done? What is evaluation saying? How do we approach it going forward? What funds do we have and what funds do we need? And so, it’s a pretty comprehensive process and we’re currently in the midst of it.
Do you have a timeline of when a concept paper will be out?

No because as always you know that given that we are multiple years outside of a procurement, we anticipate there will be additional funding needed. And so, once we finalize the amount, while being in conversation with OMB about what’s needed.

Just know this will be my continuing ongoing fight to make sure that before I leave the Cornerstones and Beacons get an RFP because they need it and deserve it. What is the budget for a Beacon Community Center?
Beacon budget for FY26 was $69 million. In FY27, it’s 67 and you asked for Cornerstone, the total budget?
I didn’t but you can give it to me.
For Cornerstone?
Yeah, you can go for it.
Okay, total Cornerstone budget for 2026 is $69 million, in 2027 it’s $68 million.
Uhm, how many centers are in each borough and what borough has the highest program attendance?
I’m going to defer to our Assistant Commissioner Wanda Ascherl who will speak more into the program performance and day to day operations.

Sure, good afternoon. Uhm, we current - our largest - the borough with the most Beacon programs is Brooklyn. We have 32 in Brooklyn and then we have 25 in Queens. Bronx is 16, Manhattan is 15, and Staten Island is 4.
Poor Staten Island.
Just given the number of sites equals the number of participants that are enrolled.

That’s interesting, especially in the Bronx where we have so much high need, us being at 16. That’s an interesting number. Hmm, so that must mean when we get the new RFP, we’ll have more sites in the Bronx. That’s what I’m hearing. I don’t know if anybody else heard that. What are the current hours of operation for Beacon Community Centers?

We currently, our programs operate a minimum of 42 hours. Uhm, over six days, so Monday through Friday plus one weekend day and then, and it’s usually in the afternoons, evenings, school holidays and uhm, during the week, they start at the end of school day, so whenever the school day ends, that's when we start.

The PMMR indicates that Cornerstone programs for NYCHA residents enrolled 11,856 Summer Youth participants in the first four months and a 16 percent increase over the same period in Fiscal 2025. There is an increase in overall participation, a community anti-poverty program in the first four months of Fiscal 2026 and 11 percent when compared to the same period in Fiscal 2025. Has the agency visited the Cornerstones to address those - has the agency visited uhm, Cornerstones to address those needs? If so, what are some of the outcomes from those visits?

So, we have a team that goes out and does inspections. They conduct multiple visits throughout the year but beyond the visits, they also do a lot of coaching. So, you’ll find my team will go out there, do PD. Uhm, looking at the data, we

look at data to inform practice and any changes that the program needs to make. Uhm, we also - depending on what the area is, we also bring in our TA partners, capacity building if needed and then we also expose them to uhm various partnership opportunities and services that are being offered through our strategic partnership team. So, oftentimes, they take advantage of a lot of those opportunities.

To provide a safe space for community members and youth to spend time, Cornerstones are required to open and staff programming for more hours than they were originally produced. How have providers been compensated for the additional staffing needs?
Providers are contracted for the additional service hours and their budgets are amended accordingly for the extra hours.
So, they can amend it?
Yes.

Cornerstone providers are often caught between DYCD and NYCHA when requesting facility repairs leading to long delays. Does DYCD have a plan to make this process easier and more

efficient? If so, uhm why has this not been prioritized?

DYCD is taking a proactive and coordinated approach to improving physical conditions at our centers. We launched a centralized ticketing system a few - maybe two years ago, where providers submit their tickets. We have a team on our end that conducts visits. As soon as we get a ticket, we assess the situation and we contract it out with external vendors to go out to the site and assess the situation and have a timeline to resolve.
And this was two years ago?
About two years ago, yeah.

No, I know it’s new because it wasn’t there when I was there, so that’s good to hear. Beyond the physical impact on programming and space, delays, repairs also impacted program budgets. Cornerstone providers share that they have received violations and been fined by New York City Department of Health and the Fire Department for issues they have already reported to DYCD or other NYCHA - or NYCHA. Those violations are based on health safety regulations to keep participants and staff safe. However, inspections by DOH and FDNY do not include

communication with DYCD or NYCHA including a review open for tickets from providers requesting facility repairs. These result in Cornerstone providers assuming responsibility for all violations associated with the fine even if they’ve been actively trying to solve the issues with the city agencies. Why are Cornerstone providers required to pay fines associated with facility repairs?

Uh, CBO’s work closely with our team to notify us if there’s a violation whether it’s FDNY or DOHMH. We have a very close working relationship with the Department of Health, so that if let’s say we need to triage on the back end, we try to provide support on that perspective. Part of the reason why the violation hits the provider is because they’re stack licensed. So, as a stack license holder, they are the ones in violation of whatever the findings are. But we do work closely and DYCD is working on strengthening the documentation and improving the uhm, improving the repair tracking system and working closely with NYCHA as needed depending on the severity of the situation.

Yeah, I think it’s just unfortunate, especially like obviously everyone wants

folks to be safe but it is true, you know obviously it is a stack license and is the provider but especially when you don’t have control over spacing, uhm, it gets really hard and you feel pretty powerless when you are putting in a request and things aren’t moving and then you are then stuck paying the fine. So, uhm - uhm Cornerstone providers that have shared that they have gone through rental assistant demolition program RAD and permanent affordability commitments together PACT, conversations about the repairs to improve the facility. There is push back from developers for any repair post construction despite language outlined in community agreement. What role does DYCD play in negotiating between providers and developers doing the RAD PACT process and what role does DYCD play after the RAD PACT conversations are complete? And how does DYCD support providers in ensuring developers are not - are compliant with facility repairs?

Yes, that’s a good question. Our role is more of an advisory role. And so, when these issues come up, we have a new team, NYCHA PACT RAD team and so, we work closely with them when we have

to triage and address any issues around communication, partnerships on the ground. So, we try to navigate those. I’m not - Chair Stevens, I’m not familiar with any developers pushing back but definitely welcome like any specifics and we can help triage. I’m not as familiar with any developers pushing back currently that I know of.

Okay, we’ll get that to you because if it’s here, that means somebody said it. So, I mean, this is happening. We don’t just make these up but we’ll definitely get back to you and I guess for me is - I’ve always been curious about even - what role are you guys playing when it’s all being negotiated beforehand right? And so, even out on the backend, what role do you play when they’re negotiating with the developers when they’re transitioning to RAD or PACT? Are you guys a part of the conversation or is NYCHA the one taking the lead? Are you guys coming in after?
NYCHA usually takes the lead for sure. That’s the starting point. Oftentimes the developments that are being converted to RAD PACT, they prioritize the apartments. That’s their priority.
Obviously hmm, hmm.

And then they have like a snippet for centers and then they start engaging the CBO on the ground. Uhm, we have a standing bimonthly I think, yeah, I think it’s monthly, a standing monthly meeting where we check in on anything that’s being converted. We have a list of sites that have been converted. We have upcoming -
Could you share that list with us please, the Committee?
Yeah.
Thank you. Not today, if you don’t have it, you could just submit it.
I know. I have to write myself a note.

Don’t worry, Andrea already wrote it down. Uhm, New York City - NYCHA Summer program at seven days a week from 6-10 with limited staff, although required. What is the number of open positions for the Cornerstones? Is there a delay in the hiring process? If so, why and what is the retention rate?

Cornerstones are funded to operate a full summer program beginning at 8 a.m.

through evening. They adhere to the SEC ratios. Staffing human services programs has been a challenge particularly during COVID but we’ve seen some improvement. Staff retention rates may vary by CBO provider but we’re not aware of any systematic delays.
Can you guys hear me?
Yes.

Okay. You can’t hear me through the mic? You guys hear me through the mic? It’s so crazy because I can hear through this so that’s why I can’t hear. Okay, hold on. I can hear here so we can hear on Zoom. Hello? Does that sound better? No, it’s okay, I can do both, it’s double time. Uhm, I don’t think I heard your answer because - so we’re asking about the retention rate uhm, of the cornerstone for staff.
So, uhm, staff retention rates vary by CBO but we’re not aware of any systematic delays at this time.

Currently Cornerstone rates the group leaders at $20 per hour and $17.50 per hour for other staff. What are the plans to increase

those rates or is there any plan to increase those rates?

So as we are looking across the agency's portfolio, we are reviewing a number of programs and contracts including Beacon, Cornerstone, and others to understand where updates and procurements need to be prioritized. Uhm, the goal is obviously to move forward in a thoughtful way that reflects provider input, coordination, along the lines of what the Commissioner shared earlier.
And the model for the Cornerstone is still the one time full time person and everyone else part time. Is that still the structure of the program?
You have a full time -
Director.
Director. You have custodial personnel.
But the only full time person is still the Director, correct?
Yes.

That was the question, thank you. And why is that? Because you know, I know everybody knows my history by now but it takes a

lot to run a Cornerstone a lot and so, we don’t think that they need additional full time staff to kind of support the capacity and also to prevent the burnout, especially during the summer when they’re supposed to be open seven days a week and late night and -

Yeah, they definitely stagger the staff to try and make sure that it’s always, there was a supervisor on site, however, that is one of the things that we are looking at as we think about you know program models in an

Oh, yeah, when the new RFP comes out, yeah. Let’s talk about it. Let’s talk it into existence because I think that that’s something we definitely need to look at, especially around like just quality of care and like burnout when we’re thinking about staff and I ran a cornerstone. I was there all the time. I did not have a life because even if I had staff there, I’m like, the building is opening, I got to come and so, I think that we got to really think about quality of life and burnout for staff and making sure that we’re able to retain quality staff. Alright, we’re going to move onto COMPASS. The anticipated contract terms for COMPASS is to be for

the six years and one month from August 1, 2026 to August 31, 2032 with no option for renewal. Is DYCD working with MOCS to implement a process in preparation for pending awards and contract negotiations?

I’ll respond, if we go further, I’ll call ACCO(SP?) back up here but we are working diligently with MOCS in every oversight to see what we can do to make sure we land this on time so that providers get registered and get their funds.
Is there a contingency plan if we don’t land this on time?

I think that if we don’t get it on time, we’ll utilize every resource he has, whether it be existing contracts or loans. And so, we want to make this happen. I think that you know we’ve all been fighting for this, the sector has been fighting and so, we’re finally here and we want to make sure that we make it happen so that people get their funds and we serve more families.

No, I know you guys are working really hard and this has been like all hands on deck situation but it is a tall task and a lot to do and a lot to roll out and so you know please

continue to let us know how we can support with this rollout. There were Council awarded funding after school providers that were not in previous COMPASS RFP’s. Are they included in this new COMPASS RFP?
This is an open procurement so every provider was open to apply if they were interested.

Well, I hope you guys pick them up because we ain’t picking them up this time. Like, could you all pick them up please? Thanks. They’ve been on our budget for awhile now. What is the response rate for the providers submissions to the new COMPASS RFP?

I will refer to our ACCO to speak more to the existing RFP but I want to speak that it’s still open so we cannot, you know, speak too much to it but I’m going to defer to her for the additional technical question.
You just come to the other side, why you keep going back? Your seats over here. They keep working these one seats.
Welcome back.
Thank you. Can you repeat the question again please?
Uhm, what is the response rate for the providers submission for the new COMPASS RFP and the next question is, what is the number of new providers versus existing provider submission to date?

Well, the RFP is currently in the active status. We have received over 1,400 proposals. Uhm, and as far as new providers rate, as submissions at this point, it was 45 percent submissions for the school base and 50 percent submissions for center based RFP of new providers.

During the September 18th after school COMPASS oversight, the agency recognized how communities have changed since the last RFP. What with that knowledge is DYCD taking a look at all the outstanding RFP to address the changes, not only in the missed communities or geographical gaps but also the necessary financial changes to accommodate the providers?
I’ll jump in. So, I think for every procurement, really we have a racial equity process. We look at existing resources agencywide and from there we decide how we allocate them.
How many of the 5,000 seats for school year 2026 have been filled to date? What are the school districts occupying the highest number of seats and which are the least seats? Is there a waitlist?
Are you referencing COMPASS?

Yes, COMPASS and so I think we’re gonna - yeah he’s back. That’s why I said just move over there. I don’t know why you all keep moving. I don’t know why it’s three empty seats. I’m just saying, I don’t know. We’re almost done with COMPASS, so you don’t have to come but Darryl, you could just start making your way soon and Susan, RHY is coming up. I know who is coming.
I’m sorry Chair, can you repeat the question again?

Uhm, where was - now I’m stressed out. I don’t know what question since I started moving. Oh, how many of the 5,000 seats for the school year 2026 have been filled to date and what are the school districts occupying the highest number of seats and which are the least seats and is there a waitlist?

So, we are excited to say that all of the schools are fully enrolled, 5,000 seats. There are 40 schools across the five boroughs. We can provide a breakout by school district and by borough with those numbers as well, and we know on the ground we’ll have to follow up on the waitlist numbers but fully enrolled programs across the board.
How many positions will be added to support the additional COMPASS elementary seats and what are those positions?
I will take that question. So, we were given an additional headcount of about 54 new positions to support the COMPASS expansion.
How many of the 5,000 seats have been provided for special needs students and have any additional accommodations been given to providers?

So, we’ll have to follow up with you on the breakout on the number of special needs youth but we do coordinate with Public Schools on any student that is enrolled in our program that will need any additional assistance.

Okay. There wasn’t designated seats specifically for students with

disabilities in this RFP? Like, there wasn’t because I know there’s a different price per point for our students with disabilities.
Price per participant, it’s a set number.
So, we don’t have it distinguished between uhm students with disabilities and uhm, general ed students?
